# AI Agents Are Already Working in Cities, Hospitals, and Sports

> **In short:** Companies including NVIDIA and Salesforce have announced AI agents being deployed across cities, hospitals, a Premier League football club, and software development teams — moving agents from experiments to services that touch real people.

You may have already spoken with an AI agent today without realizing it. An **AI agent** is software that can take actions on its own, not just answer questions — a small digital helper that can complete tasks across multiple systems, like looking things up or pulling information together. Lately, companies have been rolling them out in places most people don't think about as "AI territory."

**In European cities**, NVIDIA's recent announcement describes local governments and their software partners using NVIDIA accelerated computing (specialized hardware that runs AI faster than regular chips) to build physical AI agents and **digital twins** (virtual models of real-world systems, used to simulate changes before they're actually made). The example the company gives: helping teams decide things like when to repair a road or how to use less energy.

**In cancer care**, the picture is more cautious. According to a healthcare-focused announcement, the company describes its agentic AI as "closing oncology's data gaps" from drug discovery through to survivorship care. The idea is to connect information that today sits in separate systems, so the right data reaches the right person at the right time. Specific deployments and results aren't named in the announcement, so treat the broader picture as the company's claim rather than a confirmed rollout. *This article is not medical advice — for any health-related questions, please consult a qualified professional.*

**In football**, the picture is much more concrete. According to Salesforce's announcement, Tottenham Hotspur plans to launch "Ask Spurs" on Salesforce's Agentforce platform. The company says the new agent would unify data from over 4.6 million fan accounts across more than 10 systems, and Salesforce reports an 86% engagement rate. What that looks like for a fan: one chat for tickets, merchandise, and match info, instead of being bounced between sites.

**In software development**, a recent announcement titled "Scaling agent teams: reach the frontier at 30% of the cost" raises a different question. Coding agents are already building large-scale software — the open issue is how to organize teams of them so they don't step on each other's work.

## What this means for you

- **If you deal with city services or hospitals**: The next time you fill out a form online or chase a missing appointment, there's a growing chance an AI agent is part of the workflow behind the scenes. It usually won't announce itself.
- **If you're a sports fan**: Services like the planned Ask Spurs show where customer support is heading — one chat, less bouncing. If you're curious, the Tottenham Hotspur site or app is a place to watch for it. The company hasn't said yet which other clubs will follow.
- **If you work in any business with lots of internal systems**: The pattern across all four announcements is the same — connecting existing data so agents can act on it. That's the part most worth watching, because it's what makes an agent useful instead of just a demo.
- **If you're just curious about AI**: You don't need to "learn agents." When you meet one, it'll usually look like a chatbot — the difference is that it can actually do something for you, not just answer questions.
- **If you already use it**: Notice how every announcement names specific systems being connected (10+ at Spurs, oncology records, city operations). If an agent gives you a bad answer, the data behind it is usually the first place to look.

## Wrap-up

AI agents aren't a "someday" story — they're being deployed this month, by companies you've heard of, in services you may already use. The shift to notice: the next time a chatbot feels surprisingly helpful, it may be an agent doing the work in the background. Next time you open a chat to ask about a delivery or a hospital appointment, pause for a moment — what you're talking to may already be an agent.
